Satoru-kun: Why Japan’s All-Knowing Caller Must Stand Behind You

Call him from a public phone and he may answer the one question no human can. The price is not money. It is the shrinking distance announced by every return call.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published and updated November 13, 2026

The ritual sounds like a machine built from two obsolete futures. Put a 10-yen coin into a public telephone. Call your own mobile. Speak Satoru-kun’s name into the connection, hang up, and wait. Within a day, the story says, your phone will ring. A boyish voice gives his location. Later he calls again. Each location is closer.

Eventually the voice says it is directly behind you. Only then may you ask your question. Satoru-kun supposedly knows anything: tomorrow’s news, a lost object, the truth another person conceals. But the rules turn knowledge into danger. Do not look back. Do not fail to ask. In some tellings, do not test him with an answer you already know.

This is a legend, not a verified supernatural event, and its instructions vary sharply. That variation is our best evidence. Satoru-kun is less a fixed character than a compact story-engine that joins a payphone, a private mobile number, a forbidden glance and the oldest human temptation: wanting certainty.

10 yenThe coin most often named in retellings; it anchors the tale in an ordinary public-phone action.
24 hoursA common deadline, not a verified or universal rule. Some versions simply say the return call comes later.
1 questionThe usual reward after the caller arrives, though some retellings allow repeated advice before the final approach.

What remains stable—and what keeps moving

Across accessible retellings, the recurring core is easy to recognize: a caller named Satoru is deliberately summoned; calls report a decreasing distance; the last call places him behind the summoner; a question may then be answered. Almost everything around that core can change. The invocation is longer or shorter. A mobile is switched off—or impossibly rings while off. Satoru gives one answer or several. Looking back leads to disappearance, death, or an unspecified “other place.”

Story elementCommon versionWhat the variation reveals
InvitationPublic phone calls the summoner’s mobileThe legend needs old and new networks to touch.
ReturnSeveral calls announce closer placesRepetition turns remote voice into physical pursuit.
RewardOne truthful answerCuriosity makes the danger voluntarily chosen.
TabooDo not turn aroundThe unseen answerer remains more powerful than any fixed face.

No dependable primary document currently establishes a single creator, first post or hometown. A 2018 magazine article quoting contemporary-monster researcher Asato Itsuki presents Satoru-kun as an “IT yōkai” and records the payphone-to-smartphone pattern. Reference works and later online archives confirm circulation, but they do not prove one original script. Japan Unfolded therefore treats exact words, punishments and origin claims as variants—not instructions and not history.

The answer to the title: distance is the real monster

The surprising feature is not that Satoru-kun knows everything. Folktales are full of prophetic beings. The innovation is how the story makes an information network betray its purpose. A telephone lets a distant person arrive as sound while the body stays safely elsewhere. Satoru-kun reverses that contract: every new piece of information proves that the body is coming too.

“I’m at the station” is useful information. “I’m outside your house” is surveillance. “I’m behind you” abolishes the final boundary between communication and presence. The phone does not merely carry the haunting; its normal ability to report location becomes the countdown.

Why must he be behind you?Because an all-knowing figure would become ordinary the moment the story gave him a stable face. The taboo against looking preserves the unknown while forcing the summoner to trust a disembodied voice. Knowledge is offered at the precise moment verification becomes forbidden.

This design recalls “Mary-san’s telephone,” another Japanese legend in which a discarded doll calls from progressively closer locations and ends with “I’m behind you.” Satoru-kun adds a bargain after that famous ending: instead of pure pursuit, the final arrival opens a question-and-answer session. It also resembles Kokkuri-san and other divination games, which organize uncertainty through a repeatable procedure. But Satoru-kun is solitary and portable. The circle around a paper oracle has collapsed into one person’s handset.

A legend born between two phone eras

The tale’s hardware gives it a historical atmosphere even when no first telling can be dated. NTT East’s official data show Japan had 717,470 public telephones in fiscal 1999 and 673,041 in fiscal 2000. The network then contracted rapidly: 445,978 remained in fiscal 2003. Meanwhile personal mobile subscriptions were becoming ordinary. The legend imagines a narrow window when almost anyone recognized both the green street phone and the intensely private device in a pocket.

Public phones were shared, exposed and only partly private. Mobiles were personal, address-booked and carried home. Calling the second from the first crosses a social boundary as well as a technical one. The summoner seems to create a closed loop—my call to my number—but the legend inserts an unknown participant inside it.

Today the hardware feels almost archaeological. NTT’s 2022 outlook projected the combined number of first-category public phones operated by NTT East and West to fall from about 109,000 through fiscal 2021 to about 30,000 by fiscal 2031. That decline does not kill the story. It makes the green phone a readymade liminal object: familiar, public, useful in disasters, yet unusual enough that younger listeners may experience it as a portal from another communications age.

Is the name connected to the yōkai satori?

The resemblance is tempting. Satoru can evoke “to understand,” while the mountain creature called satori is famous for reading human thoughts. The International Research Center for Japanese Studies’ yōkai database preserves records of satori traditions, and scholarship traces how that older mind-reading figure changed in modern fiction.

But a meaningful resemblance is not proof of descent. No source located for this article demonstrates that Satoru-kun’s creator deliberately modernized the satori. The safest conclusion is narrower: the name fits the function beautifully, which may help the legend stick. It also sounds like an ordinary boy’s name. The uncanny power hides behind the friendly suffix -kun, often used for boys or younger males.

Why the promise is more frightening now

An all-knowing caller once resembled an oracle. In an age of recommendation engines, location sharing and assistants that answer instantly, he also resembles an interface. The legend asks what we surrender when a system promises frictionless certainty. Satoru-kun never demands a password in the story. The caller volunteered a number, initiated contact and kept answering.

That does not make the tale a literal prophecy about artificial intelligence. It does explain its renewed force for overseas readers. The horror is consent followed by loss of control: you ask for an answer, then discover that the answerer has been mapping the route to you.

How to explore it without reenacting it

Do not call strangers, misuse emergency equipment, obstruct a public phone, or circulate someone else’s number as part of a “challenge.” No supernatural claim has been verified, but harassment, anxiety and nuisance calls are real. The culturally useful experiment is comparison: read two versions and underline what changed. Did Satoru offer advice before arriving? Did the phone ring while powered off? What was the punishment? Each addition shows what a community wanted the story to fear.
